readerTitle: Why Facebook first opened to just one college
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Facebook의 단계별 확장) + 실제 관찰 (식당의 소프트 오프닝 관행) + 가상 적용 (학생용 앱, 라멘 가게)
insight: 출시는 하루의 행사가 아니라 순서다. 각 단계는 다음 단계에 필요한 것(밀도, 처리 능력, 개선, 입소문)을 만들어 준다.
misconception: 첫날 최대한 넓고 크게 터뜨려야 출시가 성공한다.

sources.text: Meta (Facebook) company history: launch at Harvard (Feb 2004), expansion to other colleges, high schools (2005) and open registration (Sept 2006)
Restaurant soft openings: common industry practice, described generally
학생용 앱과 라멘 가게 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Facebook 연표 확인: 2004년 2월 하버드 출시, 2004년 3월 Columbia·Stanford·Yale로 확장, 2005년 9월 고등학교 개방, 2006년 9월 13세 이상 이메일 보유자 누구나 가입 가능. 게시 전 Meta 공식 자료로 날짜를 다시 확인하세요.
Facebook이 캠퍼스 단위로 확장한 이유(친구 밀도, 서버 부담)는 널리 알려진 해석입니다. 카드에는 회사의 공식 의도로 단정하지 않고 '단계가 만들어 준 효과'로 서술했습니다.
수치(가입자 수, 비율)는 출처마다 달라 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 추가할 경우 1차 출처가 필요합니다.
소프트 오프닝 관행은 일반적 서술이며 특정 식당 사례나 통계를 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Facebook first opened to just one college
body: In February 2004, Facebook launched with a strange limit. Only students with a Harvard email address could join.
No ads. No national push. Two and a half years passed before anyone with an email address could sign up. That slow order was not caution. It was the plan.

image.label: One lit-up college building among many dark ones
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 대학 건물 여러 채가 지도 위에 흩어져 있고, 한 채만 불이 켜져 있음. 다른 건물로 향하는 점선 화살표가 희미하게. 실제 로고나 학교 문장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You have one launch budget.
body: You built an app that helps students find study partners in the same course. It only works if enough classmates are on it.
You have money and staff for one launch push. How do you spend it?

options.text: Launch nationwide with ads to reach as many students as possible
options.feedback: You get the biggest headline, but users land on a near-empty app. Each person finds few classmates, and many never come back.

options.text: Launch at one university, make it work there, then move to the next
options.feedback: You give up early reach to get a full, useful app in one place. That success becomes your pitch to the next campus.

options.text: Launch at ten universities at once with a smaller push at each
options.feedback: Safer than nationwide, and you learn faster across schools. But spread thin, no campus may reach the point where the app feels alive.

cards.title: Facebook opened one door at a time.
body: Each step added a group only after the last one was working. A new campus joined a product that already had a track record.

breakdown.label: Anyone 13+
breakdown.detail: Open to everyone with an email

cards.title: Launch sequencing
body: **Launch sequencing** means planning the order of your rollout so each stage builds what the next stage needs.

A launch is not one day. It's a series of steps: a small group first, then a larger one, then the full market. The question is not just *who* goes first, but what each step must prove or create before you take the next.

image.label: A staircase where each step is labeled with what it unlocks
image.brief: 계단 인포그래픽. 아래부터 "Small group", "Next group", "Full market". 각 계단 옆에 작은 아이콘과 라벨: "Proof", "Fixes", "Capacity", "Word of mouth". 위로 갈수록 계단이 넓어짐.

cards.title: What each stage buys you.
body: A good early stage hands the next one something it can't get any other way:
list: **Density:** enough people in one place for the product to feel full
**Fixes:** problems found while the audience is small and forgiving
**Capacity:** time to grow servers, staff or supply before demand spikes
**Proof and word of mouth:** a story the next group has already heard
cards.callout: Skip a stage and the next one starts without these.

cards.title: Restaurants have done this for decades.
body: Many restaurants open quietly before their grand opening. A friends-and-family night, then a few weeks with a short menu and limited hours.
The kitchen learns its timing. Staff learn the room. Dishes that don't work get cut. Only then do they invite press and run the big opening.
The logic matches Facebook's: a small, forgiving audience first, so the big audience meets a finished product.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams often release a new feature to a small share of users first, then widen it step by step. If something breaks, it breaks for a few people, not everyone.

cards.title: Slow can cost you too.
body: Every stage takes time. A rival with a faster, broader launch may grab the market you were saving for later.
Early stages can also mislead. Friends and loyal fans are kinder than strangers, so a great soft launch may not predict a great full launch.
And some launches can't be staged well, such as a product tied to one season or event. Sequence when each step clearly feeds the next, not out of nerves.

cards.title: Now it's a ramen shop.
body: You're opening a ramen shop. A well-known food writer offers to visit in your first week. A local influencer wants to host a big opening-day event.
Your kitchen team has never cooked together at full speed. What's your order?

options.text: Big opening day with the influencer, food writer in week one
options.feedback: You get maximum early attention. But the busiest, most-watched nights come before the kitchen has found its rhythm, and first reviews stick.

options.text: Two weeks of soft opening with a short menu, then the writer and the big event
options.feedback: You trade a little early buzz for a tested kitchen. The writer and the crowd meet the shop at its best.

options.text: Soft open with no end date, and wait to invite press until it feels perfect
options.feedback: The kitchen gets plenty of practice, but rent keeps running and the opening momentum fades. A stage needs a goal and an end.

cards.title: Launch in an order where each step feeds the next.
body: Before a launch, ask what the next stage needs and which earlier stage will create it.
**Try it today:** write your next launch as three steps. Next to each, write one thing it must prove or build before you move on.
